templates.pattern: A channel has a bandwidth of [B] MHz and a signal-to-noise ratio of [SNR]. Calculate the Shannon channel capacity in Mbits/s.
templates.explanation:
Shannon capacity C = B × log₂(1 + SNR)
= [B] × log₂(1 + [SNR])
= [B] × log₂([SNR+1])
= [RESULT] Mbits/s

This is the theoretical maximum data rate. SNR values chosen give exact log₂ results: SNR=1→log₂(2)=1, SNR=3→log₂(4)=2, SNR=7→log₂(8)=3 etc.

templates.pattern: A channel has a bandwidth of [B] MHz and uses [V] signal levels. Calculate the Nyquist data rate in Mbits/s.
templates.explanation:
Nyquist rate = 2 × B × log₂(V)
= 2 × [B] × log₂([V])
= 2 × [B] × [log2(V)]
= [RESULT] Mbits/s

The Nyquist theorem gives the maximum data rate for a noiseless channel. More signal levels increase the data rate but require better signal quality.

templates.pattern: A signal has a signal power of [S] mW and noise power of [N] mW. Calculate the signal-to-noise ratio in decibels.
templates.explanation:
SNR (dB) = 10 × log₁₀(S ÷ N)
= 10 × log₁₀([S] ÷ [N])
= 10 × log₁₀([S/N])
= [RESULT] dB

The decibel scale is logarithmic. An SNR of 10 dB means the signal is 10 times stronger than the noise. Higher SNR means better quality signal.

templates.pattern: A network link has a throughput of [THRU] Mbits/s and a bandwidth of [BW] Mbits/s. Calculate the bandwidth efficiency as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Bandwidth efficiency = (throughput ÷ bandwidth) × 100
= ([THRU] ÷ [BW]) × 100
= [RESULT]%

Bandwidth efficiency measures how effectively the available bandwidth is being used. Overhead, errors and protocol limitations all reduce efficiency below 100%.

templates.pattern: A TCP connection has a window size of [W] KB and a round trip time of [RTT] ms. Calculate the maximum TCP throughput in KB/s.
templates.explanation:
TCP throughput = window size ÷ RTT
= [W] KB ÷ ([RTT] ÷ 1000) s
= [W] × 1000 ÷ [RTT]
= [RESULT] KB/s

TCP throughput is limited by the window size — the amount of data that can be in transit at once. A larger window or lower RTT both increase throughput.

templates.pattern: A network sends [SENT] packets and [LOST] packets are lost. Calculate the packet loss rate as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Packet loss rate = (lost packets ÷ sent packets) × 100
= ([LOST] ÷ [SENT]) × 100
= [RESULT]%

Packet loss causes retransmissions which reduce throughput. TCP detects packet loss through timeouts and duplicate acknowledgements and reduces its transmission rate.

templates.pattern: A link has a transmission delay of [TRANS] ms and a propagation delay of [PROP] ms. Calculate the link utilisation as a percentage.
templates.explanation:
Link utilisation = transmission delay ÷ (transmission + propagation) × 100
= [TRANS] ÷ ([TRANS] + [PROP]) × 100
= [TRANS] ÷ [TRANS+PROP] × 100
= [RESULT]%

High utilisation means the link is busy sending data most of the time. Low utilisation means the link is idle waiting for propagation.

templates.pattern: A wireless signal has a frequency of [F] GHz. Calculate the wavelength of the signal in metres. (speed of light = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
templates.explanation:
Wavelength λ = c ÷ f
= 3 × 10⁸ ÷ ([F] × 10⁹)
= 3 ÷ ([F] × 10)
= 0.3 ÷ [F]
= [RESULT] m

Higher frequency signals have shorter wavelengths. Wi-Fi uses 2.4 GHz (λ≈0.125m) and 5 GHz (λ≈0.06m). Higher frequencies carry more data but are absorbed more easily.

templates.pattern: A wireless signal has a wavelength of [LAM] cm. Calculate the frequency of the signal in GHz. (speed of light = 3 × 10⁸ m/s)
templates.explanation:
Frequency f = c ÷ λ
= 3 × 10⁸ ÷ ([LAM] × 10⁻²)
= 3 × 10⁸ ÷ [LAM/100] m
= [RESULT] GHz

Frequency and wavelength are inversely related. Shorter wavelengths mean higher frequencies and more data capacity.

templates.pattern: A network sends [SENT] packets. The packet loss rate is [LOSS]%. Calculate the number of packets successfully received.
templates.explanation:
Packets received = total sent × (1 − loss rate)
= [SENT] × (100 − [LOSS]) ÷ 100
= [SENT] × [100-LOSS] ÷ 100
= [RESULT]

Even a small packet loss rate significantly impacts application performance. Video streaming requires less than 1% loss while voice calls can tolerate up to 5% loss.
